source.title: Avoiding Spurious Local Minima in Deep Quadratic Networks.
source.authors: A. Kazemipour; Brett W. Larsen; Shaul Druckmann

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some extracted mathematical symbols and equations are garbled, but the relevant experiment descriptions and conclusions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether gradient-based optimization reaches global minima in quadratic networks, using synthetic regression and binary MNIST experiments rather than the claim’s CIFAR classification settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own optimization outcomes for modified and unmodified quadratic networks, including MNIST classification tasks trained as regression. Cited Zhang et al. results are prior work and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study establishes and measures global regression optimization in specially modified quadratic networks. These results do not test CIFAR convolutional classification error (V1), ReLU teacher-student width effects (V2), or the mechanisms specified in V3–V6. It cites V1's original finding as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors characterize quadratic-network MSE landscapes and argue that sufficient width combined with a data-norm regressor or orthogonality regularization permits escape from spurious stationary points and convergence to global minima. Experiments support global regression optimization on synthetic and binary MNIST tasks. The detailed deep-network theorem allows nonglobal stationary points with negative curvature; it does not establish that every stationary point is globally optimal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses quadratic activations and QL networks with an added data-norm regressor or orthogonality penalty, optimized with ADAM. The MNIST classification tasks are trained as regression. It does not test standard ReLU or convolutional benchmark recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcomes are reported across data-generation settings and network width; the paper also distinguishes modified networks from an unmodified quadratic network. In the deep synthetic experiments, empirical global minima are reached at widths below the theoretical threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Modified single-QL-layer quadratic networks reach the least-squares regression optimum for k ≥ d across planted and independent-output synthetic data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding a trainable data-norm regressor enables the tested quadratic networks to reach global regression minima at sufficient width.

fits_no_version.finding: Unmodified quadratic networks exhibit spurious local minima.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width alone does not eliminate spurious local minima in quadratic networks with trainable output weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Two-QL-layer networks with an orthogonality penalty attain least-squares regression optima on synthetic and binary MNIST tasks, including below the theoretical width threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested penalized deep quadratic networks reach global regression optima with fewer intermediate units than the sufficient theoretical bound.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 displays training and generalization classification accuracy for quadratic networks trained on binary MNIST regression targets; numerical accuracies are unreadable in the supplied text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quadratic networks trained by regression can perform binary classification on PCA-reduced MNIST.

record.problems: Experiments are on synthetic regression and PCA-reduced binary MNIST regression, not CIFAR classification. Theoretical guarantees depend on special quadratic architectures and modifications. Classification accuracy is displayed only in a figure without textual values. Reported outcomes aggregate repeated trials; the MNIST description reports 50 realizations but gives no numerical error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Figure 3 and Figures 4–5 show additional width-specific curves, but the text reports the aggregate conclusions rather than numerical points; the figure-only classification accuracy is retained as R9–R10 because it is a distinct measure relevant to the claim's subject.

untested.parts: All specified convolutional CIFAR training-error results, including corrupted labels and model-size or regularization qualifications.
ReLU teacher-student problems, joint teacher/student growth, and adding one or two student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain convolutional networks and its prevention by identity shortcuts or the specified initialization recipes.
Activation-matched signal propagation, comparative training speed and depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Loss and curvature trajectories relative to learning-rate stability thresholds, recovery, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons in training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: States marked cannot_determine concern the supplied claim versions; they do not negate the study's reported quadratic-regression findings. Initialization requirements within these modified quadratic objectives do not independently test V4's signal-propagation and training-speed claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sufficiently large convolutional networks, CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, SGD or Adam classification error as specified in the version. Its two binary MNIST tasks are regression objectives, and the paper reports classification accuracy but not training classification error.
